one_liner: RANLUX recast as a 576-bit LCG with x86-64 assembly modmul; about 8x faster than classic RANLUX implementations.
what_it_does: Implements Sibidanov's RANLUX++: the subtract-with-borrow RANLUX generator rewritten as an LCG x <- A*x mod (2^576 - 2^240 + 1), where A = a^p folds RANLUX's skipping (default p = 2048) into one multiplier. The ranluxpp class returns floats or doubles in [0,1) through operator()(float) / operator()(double) tag overloads, bulk getarray(n, ptr), seeding by a 2^96*seed jump, jump(n) and setskip(n). The repo also ships an optimized conventional RANLUX (scalar, SSE2 and AVX2 multi-lane classes, plus a James-compatible FORTRAN emulation) and std:: engine benchmarks.
how_it_is_fast: Classic RANLUX generates and throws away most of its subtract-with-borrow outputs to decorrelate them; the LCG view replaces all that skipping with a single 576x576-bit modular multiplication. That multiply is hand-written AT&T x86-64 assembly (schoolbook, 81 64x64 products) with mulx and adcx/adox variants picked by GCC function multiversioning, plus a reduction specialized to the sparse modulus: 155 cycles per modmul on Skylake per the README. One modmul yields 24 floats (24-bit) or 11 doubles (52-bit) unpacked directly from the state bits.
when_to_use: HEP, lattice or other Monte Carlo codes that must use a RANLUX-family generator for its theoretical mixing guarantees and are bottlenecked by std::ranlux24/48 or James-style RANLUX (TRandom1)
x86-64 Linux with GCC, where the assembly and function multiversioning build as shipped
Many independent streams: seeds map to jumps of 2^96*seed states, and jump(n) skips n RANLUX numbers in O(log n) modmuls
Research or testing that needs the RANLUX-to-LCG state mapping (getlcgstate / getranluxseq) or a fast reference to check another RANLUX++ port against
when_not_to_use: Throughput-first simulations: RANLUX++ is still slower than Mersenne Twister (ROOT measured TRandom3 at about 3 ns versus about 8 ns), and xoshiro/PCG/Philox are faster still

Non-x86-64 targets, Windows/MSVC, or non-GCC toolchains: the assembly uses the System V register ABI and the dispatch relies on GCC target attributes; ROOT's portable RanluxppEngine (about 9 ns after tuning on the same Ryzen) or Randompack's MIT ranlux++ cover those cases

Code that needs bit-exact RANLUX output or the full theoretical guarantees: ROOT's reimplementation documents fixes to this code (canonical modulo result, converting the LCG state back to RANLUX numbers to avoid a bias in the upper state bits, 48 rather than 52 bits per double)
Projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0-or-later or an unmaintained dependency (last commit 2018-01-17, 6 commits)
Code that expects a std:: engine: there is no result_type/min()/max() interface, so <random> distributions cannot use it directly

integration.form: static lib (Makefile builds libranlux++.a from C++ and GNU as assembly)
integration.dependencies: none beyond GCC and GNU as
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with function multiversioning (target("arch=...") overloads); C++11 delegating constructors plus GNU extensions (__attribute__, __builtin_expect, hex-float literals); exact GCC version not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 only (System V ABI assembly); the Makefile builds everything with -mavx2, so the shipped build needs an AVX2 CPU even though mul9x9mod has a generic fallback
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; all state (LCG words, multiplier, float/double caches) is per instance, so use one object per thread

gotchas: Outputs are unpacked from the LCG state, not from the RANLUX base-2^24 sequence, so the numbers differ from std::ranlux24/48 and TRandom1 even when the states are equivalent; primitive() changes the multiplier to a^2048 + 13, which leaves RANLUX equivalence altogether

init(seed) multiplies the current state instead of resetting to x_0, and it does not clear the float/double caches, so reseeding a used object does not reach the documented x_0*A^(2^96*seed) state (read from src/ranluxpp.cxx)

Multiversion dispatch is keyed to arch=haswell/broadwell/skylake; GCC selects arch= versions by CPU model, so other CPUs (AMD Zen, newer Intel cores) likely run the generic mul path (inferred from src/mulmod.cxx, not documented)

operator() reinterprets a uint32_t/uint64_t cache as float/double through pointer casts (a strict-aliasing violation) and is marked noinline, so per-call overhead is a real function call; getarray is the fast path
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other catalogued sibling is a RANLUX-family generator except Randompack, whose MIT-licensed ranlux++ engine is reported (per a search snippet of its paper) to be as fast as or up to 2x faster than this code; pick this repo only as the reference assembly on x86-64 Linux with GCC. If RANLUX-grade theory is not required, xoshiro, PCG or Philox siblings (e.g. benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD, simdrng) are several times faster.
verified_claims_summary: A ROOT developer measured Sibidanov's assembly implementation at about 8 ns per number against about 62 ns for ROOT's TRandom1 RANLUX (single precision only) on one core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900, CentOS 8.2, GCC 8.3.1, 10 repetitions with under 1% standard deviation, flags not stated (about 7.8x, derived from page data). The README's own figure, 20 versus 198 clocks per float against GCC's std RANLUX on Haswell, is first-party, mixes CPUs and does not say whether ranlux24 or ranlux48 was timed.
status_note: Abandoned since January 2018 (6 commits) and LGPL-3.0-or-later; the algorithm lives on in ROOT 6.24+ (TRandomRanluxpp / RanluxppEngine, portable and with correctness fixes) and in Randompack's MIT reimplementation, which are the better choices for new code.
